name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 26 May 1990 (English cryptic)

clue.text: Help rejected by race with invective

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back the way it came, so the word for help is read backwards

blocks.note: aid is help
a tribe is a race or people

explanation.surface: Someone refused assistance because of their ethnicity, and abusive language came with it.
explanation.definitionFit: A diatribe is a bitter verbal attack, which is what invective means: abusive, denunciatory speech.

clue.text: French actress in strange muddle — no such here!

definitions.text: French actress in strange muddle — no such here!

indicators.note: strange means odd or altered, so these letters are mixed into a new order
in places the actress inside the scrambled letters

blocks.note: BB, Brigitte Bardot's initials, by which she was famous
letters to rearrange
letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A French film star in a confused state, with a cheeky aside to the solver.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well as the wordplay: a muddled screen siren, and the setter jokes that no solver is one.
explanation.definitionFit: A dumb blonde is the stereotype of an unintelligent fair-haired woman, which the setter insists solvers are not.

clue.text: Rat a sheriffs band caught at it by accident

indicators.note: letters landing by accident fall into a random order, so they must be rearranged
something caught is held inside, so the band surrounds the rearranged letters

blocks.note: taken as written
a posse is a band of men summoned by a sheriff
letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sheriff's posse catches a rat red-handed purely by chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rat' looks like the creature caught by the posse, but it is the verb: to desert one's side.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat is to desert or betray one's cause, and to apostatise is to abandon one's faith or party.

clue.text: 23 students made to flout the rules

indicators.note: made means fashioned or built into something new, so the letters are refashioned into another word

blocks.note: 23 down is a drink
L is the learner's plate, standing for a student

explanation.surface: Students fuelled by drink end up breaking the rules.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebel is to resist authority, and flouting the rules is an act of defiance of that kind.

clue.text: Inauspicious display of arms?

blocks.note: surface reading: an ill-omened show of weaponry
setter's reading: arms are a heraldic coat of arms, and inauspicious is the Latin-rooted word for left-handed and unlucky

explanation.surface: A military parade that bodes ill.
explanation.walkthrough: A bend is a diagonal band on a shield; the left-handed one is traditionally said to mark illegitimacy.
explanation.definitionFit: A bend sinister is a heraldic stripe on a coat of arms, and sinister also means ominous or unlucky.

clue.text: Stick the devil's brew

blocks.note: an imp is a little devil; the 's stands for 'is' or simply possession
ale is a brew

explanation.surface: A colon-like aside: something stuck in, then the devil's own brew, as if describing a witch's cauldron.
explanation.definitionFit: To impale is to stick or pierce something through with a point, so the verb stick fits as a synonym.

clue.text: Cheese for taking the mickey?

blocks.note: surface reading: some cheese to use when teasing someone
setter's reading: taking means catching and the mickey is a mouse, so the cheese is bait

explanation.surface: Which cheese suits a bit of mockery?
explanation.walkthrough: To take the mickey is British slang for teasing; read literally it is capturing a Mickey Mouse. Mousetrap is also a nickname for cheap Cheddar.
explanation.definitionFit: A mousetrap is a device baited with cheese to catch mice, and the word is also slang for plain cheese.

clue.text: Writer has friends abroad

blocks.note: first meaning: Kingsley or Martin ..., British novelists
second meaning: the French word for friends

explanation.surface: An author has pals overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: Amis is both the surname of two English novelists and the French plural for friends.

clue.text: They look to be in audible agreement

indicators.note: audible means heard, so the word is identified by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: ayes are votes of agreement

explanation.surface: People seem, from what one can hear, to be in accord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They look' reads as 'they appear', but here eyes are what look.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyes are the organs that look, so 'they look' describes them directly.

clue.text: Back-room team a bit rusty under the surface

definitions.text: a bit rusty under the surface

indicators.note: back tells the solver to take the word that follows from its end to its start

blocks.note: taken as written
a band is a group or team

explanation.surface: Office talk: the back-room staff are a little out of practice, though it hardly shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back-room team' reads as one phrase for behind-the-scenes staff; split it after 'Back', which acts on the next word alone. Moorband is a soil term, rare outside geology.
explanation.definitionFit: Moorband is a hard iron-rich soil layer, coloured like rust, that lies beneath the topsoil: a rusty stratum below ground.

clue.text: Over having sexual attraction, the priest takes the cake

indicators.note: turned over, the words that follow are read from right to left

blocks.note: Eli is the priest in the Book of Samuel, a crossword regular
a bun is a small cake

explanation.surface: A priest, tempted by allure, helps himself to the cake.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits between the reversal signal at the front and the rest of the wordplay, an unusual layout; 'Over' acts on everything after the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: Nubile describes a young woman considered sexually attractive or of marriageable age.

clue.text: Tipsy Yank driver, he could be

definitions.text: Tipsy Yank driver, he could be

indicators.note: tipsy means unsteady with drink, so the letters stagger into a new order

blocks.note: letters to rearrange
letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An American motorist who is drunk might well be a big boozer.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the anagram and the definition: a tipsy driver could be one.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy drinker is someone who regularly drinks a lot of alcohol, likely to be tipsy at the wheel.

clue.text: Field where Spooner says cows, have been?

indicators.note: Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the phrase must be said with its initial sounds exchanged

blocks.note: cows are cattle, and 'have been' becomes 's been; swap the opening B and C sounds

explanation.surface: A farmer asks which meadow the herd has been grazing in.
explanation.walkthrough: CATTLE'S BEEN spoken with the first sounds exchanged becomes BATTLE SCENE.
explanation.definitionFit: A field in the military sense is a battleground, the scene where a battle is fought.

clue.text: Jolly Roger may droop after having some of 17 in pie

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the pie

blocks.note: taken as written
17 across is NEVER MIND, built around vermin; a rat is one of the vermin
to flag is to droop or tire

explanation.surface: A pirate's banner hangs limp after vermin get into a pie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the drooping word last, behind the filled pie. The cross-reference points at the vermin inside 17 across.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jolly Roger is the skull-and-crossbones banner flown by pirate ships.

clue.text: East drives when drunk and attracts attention

indicators.note: drunk means reeling and disordered, so the letters are thrown into a different order

blocks.note: letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone drives east while drunk and draws notice to themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: To advertise is to make something publicly known, drawing notice to it.

clue.text: A host of unbridled sayings

indicators.note: unbridled means running loose without restraint, so these letters are let loose into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A great crowd of uncontrolled remarks, as at a rowdy gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: Oaths are solemn sworn statements, or curses, and either way they are things said: sayings in a loose sense.

clue.text: Sunk first course in meal with editor

indicators.note: first asks for only the opening letter of the next word
in places that letter inside the meal

blocks.note: the opening letter of course
supper is an evening meal
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: Dinner sank at the first course while the editor was present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First course' wants to be a starter, but it means only the first letter of course.
explanation.definitionFit: To scupper a ship is to sink it deliberately, so scuppered means sunk.

clue.text: Edward's infested with nasty things — but no matter

indicators.note: a thing infested has pests living inside it, so one word is filled with the other

blocks.note: Ned is a short form of Edward; the 's reads as 'is'
vermin are nasty creatures

explanation.surface: Edward's place is overrun with pests, but he shrugs it off.
explanation.definitionFit: Never mind is an idiom brushing something aside as unimportant, the same sense as 'no matter'.

clue.text: Talked about hell and uttered 15

blocks.note: Dis is the classical underworld, hell
15 across is oaths, and to utter oaths is to cuss

explanation.surface: Someone talked about hell and swore while doing it.
explanation.definitionFit: To discuss something is to talk it over, so discussed is a synonym of talked about.

clue.text: Tranquillity of champion gymnast

blocks.note: PE, physical education, is school gym; here it stands for gymnastics
an ace is a champion

explanation.surface: The serene composure of a title-winning gymnast.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'champion gymnast' as 'PE ace', a champion at gym: the two pieces go in the reverse of the clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: Peace is a state of calm and quiet, which is what tranquillity means.

clue.text: Tricky situation — somehow pride prevented religious works, as they used to say

indicators.note: somehow says the word that follows arrives at its form in some unexplained way, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
in old usage to prevent was to come before, so this supplies the verb came, placed before the next piece
NT, the New Testament, is a body of religious writings

explanation.surface: An awkward position: arrogance somehow blocked the production of sacred texts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As they used to say' flags the archaic sense of prevent, to go before, so the scrambled pride came before NT. 'Prevented' looks like stopping but means preceding.
explanation.definitionFit: A predicament is an awkward or difficult situation from which escape is hard.

clue.text: Voices of 11 the French turn up

indicators.note: in a down entry turning up flips the order so it reads from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: 11 down is a heavy drinker, a sot
la is French for the

explanation.surface: The voices of a drunk, French-speaking crowd rise.
explanation.definitionFit: Altos are singers with the voice range below soprano, and so are voices in a choir.

clue.text: A place to notice

blocks.note: first meaning: a particular location
second meaning: to catch sight of

explanation.surface: Somewhere worth paying attention to.
explanation.definitionFit: Spot is a noun for a location and a verb meaning to notice or catch sight of.

clue.text: Drink to be set before a queen

blocks.note: taken as written
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: A beverage to be served to Her Majesty.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer is an alcoholic drink brewed from malt and hops.

clue.text: Verse and essay by U.S. writer

blocks.note: Edgar Allan Poe, the American writer
an essay is an attempt, a try

explanation.surface: A poem and an essay written by an American author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essay' reads as a piece of prose but here means an attempt; the American writer goes first though 'by' places him last in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse is metrical writing, and poetry is the general name for that kind of writing.

clue.text: Idle pleasure with 23, like races organised on board

blocks.note: first meaning: 23 down is beer, and 'beer and ___' is the stock phrase for easy idle pleasure
second meaning: a game organised on a board or alley, competitive like races

explanation.walkthrough: 'Life isn't all beer and skittles' is the proverb behind the first half. The second half is loose in this scan; skittles is a pub game set up on a board or alley.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer and skittles is a fixed phrase for leisure and fun, and skittles is also a game of knocking down pins.

clue.text: One in business put one across

indicators.note: in places the first word inside the second

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
trade is business or commerce

explanation.surface: A businessman managed to trick someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: a tirade is a harangue delivered at someone, put across to them; the printed text may be garbled here.
explanation.definitionFit: A tirade is a long angry speech aimed at a listener, an outburst one puts across to them.

clue.text: Signs of the times in the Times?

definitions.text: Signs of the times in the Times?

blocks.note: surface reading: portents showing which way things are heading
setter's reading: the newspaper world is the press, and times are ages, so the word splits into those two

explanation.surface: Indicators of the era as reported in a famous newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer reads as PRES(S) AGES, the press's eras, with the shared S doing double duty; that is the joke behind 'in the Times'.
explanation.definitionFit: Presages are omens or warning signs of what is to come, signs of the times in the literal sense.
